Hello DartR team!

Thank you very much for your in depth response to my previous question about GRM network methods implemented in DartR! We have found some interesting results and would like to include some network plots in our manuscript. I was wondering if there are any advanced tinkering options for the aesthetics of the plots, such as modifying the transparency of certain nodes (e.g. 'alpha' option in ggplot2) or changing the line color/type for the connections between nodes?

Thank you!

Evan

I include in the function the parameters you suggested. To use these changes you need to install the development version of dartR by typing in the R console:

> library(dartR)
> gl.install.vanilla.dartR(flavour = "dev")

After installing, you can try:

library(dartR)
test <- platypus.gl <http://platypus.gl>
grm <- gl.grm(test,plotheatmap = FALSE,verbose = 0)
res <- gl.grm.network(grm,
                      test,
                      node.size =8,
                      node.alpha = 1/2,
                      link.color = "red",
                      link.size = 3)

Cheers,
Luis

1. The function name is gl.install.vanilla.dartR, but the function actually compares the installed packages with the the currently available ones on CRAN. Be aware this function only works if a version of dartR is already installed on your system. You can choose if you also want to have a specific version of dartR installed ('CRAN', 'master', 'beta' or 'dev' ). 'master', 'beta' and 'dev' are installed from Github. Be aware that the dev version from GitHub is not thoroughly tested and most certainly will contain untested functions.

2. For the moment, it is not possible to direct the installation done by gl.install.vanilla.dartR to a specific folder, as you commented in your previous message. Also, this function had a bug in previous versions, so I recommend just using this function using the CRAN version or the Master version.

Cheers,
Luis

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I have read that you can also filter for allele balance to eliminate false heterozygous (see OLeary et al., 2018. These aren’t the loci you’re looking for- Principles of effective SNP filtering for molecular ecologists: https://doi.org/10.1111/mec.14792):

"Allele Balance compares the number of reads for the reference allele to the number of reads for the alternate allele across heterozygotes. The expected allele balance is 0.5; large deviations may indicate false heterozygotes due to coverage effects, multilocus contigs or other artefacts."

At the moment in dartR, there is no function that does this, correct?

I guess this would mean calculating a ratio between AvgCountRef & AvgCountSnp for all heterozygous loci?

Thank you for any feedback on this.
Best,
Gabriella

pca <-  glPca(gl,

center = TRUE,
scale = FALSE,

loadings = TRUE,
alleleAsUnit = FALSE,

useC = TRUE,
returnDotProd=FALSE,
matDotProd=NULL

male.pca3 <- gl.pcoa(male.gl <http://male.gl/>, nfactors= 4)

male.pca2 <- glPca(male.gl <http://male.gl/>, center = TRUE, scale = FALSE, nf = 4, loadings = TRUE,

messages.subject: Re: [dartR] Re: Calulating global fst values
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ella,

The gl.fst.pop function is a wrapper for the function stappFst from Package StAMPP. This function uses Bootstrapping to calculate the p-values. The bootstrapping method resamples the individuals "nboots" times and calculates FST every time for each locus. Then all the calculated FST > 0 are summed and divided by "nboots" to get the p-value. In other words, the proportion of bootstrapped FST values equal to zero or less (no differentiation between populations) is used as the P-value for differentiation.

So, if all the bootstrapped FST values are zero, the p-value will be zero.

You can increase the number of bootstraps ("nboots") to be more confident in the statistical significance of your results.

Cheers,
Luis
